rationale: A wins because it keeps the story inside the facts and separates four real reporter paths: format shift, public-company margin thesis, labor risk, and a future before/after retrofit proof story. Its strongest line, "One retrofitted Sweetgreen, before and after the conveyor," is exactly the kind of trade-depth angle that knows when it is not ready yet. B has useful bones, but "$15 salad" and "premium fast-casual needs human hands" smuggle in assumptions the update did not give it, and that is how a decent pitch turns into a fact-check problem.
gaps_in_A: "robot assembly" slightly overstates the described system; the update says automated conveyor assembly, not necessarily robots.
"funding-mechanics" is the wrong story-type label for a public-company profitability angle; the substance works, but the label is sloppy.
"Decay: week" on the markets angle may be generous unless the margin disclosure is tied to a dated earnings or investor event.
gaps_in_B: "The $15 salad" is invented. No price appears in the update.
"premium, customizable, ingredient-forward" and "the tier where automation couldn't go" are unsupported category claims dressed up as insight.
"ongoing fights around restaurant-worker protections and minimum wage" is a fake external news peg unless sourced outside the supplied update.
"The belief (automation degrades premium food quality) is real" asserts a market belief the prompt did not provide. Good contrarian discipline, bad grounding.
